title: Chart Selection by Question
objective: After this lesson you will be able to map any stakeholder question to a chart family (trend/comparison/composition/relationship/distribution) and reject mismatches with the encoding reason.
why: Most bad charts are right answers to wrong mappings: pies for trends, lines for categories, 3D for everything. Selection by question class (what relationship does the question ask about?) plus encoding honesty (position/length over angle/area) makes chart choice mechanical — and mismatches reviewable with reasons, not taste.

blocks.text: **Trend** (change over time → line, ordered x). **Comparison** (magnitudes across groups → sorted bars). **Composition** (parts of wholes → stacked bars/treemap; pies only 2–4 familiar shares). **Relationship** (x vs y → scatter/heatmap + confounder brainstorm). **Distribution** (spread/shape → histogram/box). Name the family first; the chart follows.

Humans decode **position/length** precisely, **angle/area/color** poorly: sorted bars (position) > pies (angle) > bubble areas (squared lies) > 3D effects (distortion as decoration). Choose the most precise channel the question allows; relegate weak channels to secondary encoding (color for categories on positioned bars, never as the message).

blocks.title: When families collide
blocks.text: Trend-of-composition (mix over time) and distribution-comparison (spreads by group) blend families: lead with the primary question, layer the secondary (stacked areas for mix-trends, grouped boxes for group-spreads). Mixed questions get layered charts, never forced singles.

blocks.title: Route the question
blocks.note: Run it: expect 6/6 with the vague brief routing to clarify-question. Question classification precedes charting — unclassifiable briefs get clarified, never decorated.

items: Encoding hierarchy: position/length precise; angle/area weak; 3D distortion, never information
Unclassifiable briefs route to clarification, not decoration

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice router on all six briefs and map families. (b) For 'revenue mix across 12 categories', argue stacked-bars over pie with the encoding reason. (c) State what 'make it pop' needs before any chart exists.
hints: Baseline 6/6 incl. clarify-question fallback (vague briefs route out).
12-slice pies defeat angle judgment; stacked bars encode in position/length with sortability — precision argument, not taste.
Clarification: the actual question (trend? comparison?) — charting unasked questions decorates confusion.
exercise.why: Family routing (question→chart), encoding argument (precision hierarchy), and brief discipline (clarify before charting) are the three selection judgments.
exercise.code: // Selection pattern: classify question → encode precisely → clarify if unclassifiable.

quiz.q: Monthly revenue trend as a pie. Verdict?
options: Category error: trends need time-ordered lines; pies show static composition — wrong family entirely
quiz.explain: Family mismatches aren't style choices: pies can't show change over time. Classify first, chart second.

options: Quadratic lie: doubled radius quadruples area — encode in position/length or scale radius by square root with labels
quiz.explain: Area perception follows actual area: linear radius mapping squares messages. Honest channels or explicit labels.

options: Clarify the questions first: unasked briefs get questions, not decoration
quiz.explain: Decoration without questions produces impressive confusion. Family classification precedes all visual work.

summary: Classify by family, encode by precision hierarchy, clarify the unclassifiable. Selection is mechanical and reviewable — taste enters nowhere.
next: Families mapped — now their shapes: distributions with honest bins, skew, and outliers. Next: spread without lies.
